4SAFETY & RADIATION
Both studies use low-dose ⁹⁹ᵐTc tracers (bone scan effective dose ~3–4 mSv; HIDA ~2–3 mSv), comparable to a CT and far below any deterministic threshold. Patients drink fluids and void frequently after a bone scan to clear tracer from the bladder and reduce gonadal dose. There is no iodinated-contrast or nephrotoxicity concern with the tracer itself, and no thyroid blockade is required for ⁹⁹ᵐTc-MDP or HIDA (unlike free-iodide or ¹²³I studies).
🚩 Pregnancy is a relative contraindication — defer non-urgent scans; if essential, minimise activity. Breastfeeding should be interrupted (express and discard for ~12–24 h) and close contact with infants limited after injection.
🎓 High-yield triad to memorise: SUPERSCAN = diffuse skeletal uptake with "absent kidneys"; FLARE = apparent worsening early in successful treatment; HIDA non-filling gallbladder at 60 min = acute cholecystitis.

Bone scintigraphy with bone-avid radiotracers is the pivotal non-invasive test for transthyretin (ATTR) cardiac amyloidosis. Tracers designed to image the skeleton show striking, abnormal uptake in the amyloid-laden myocardium of ATTR — but characteristically NOT in AL (light-chain) amyloidosis. When combined with a negative screen for a monoclonal protein, a strongly positive scan permits a confident diagnosis of ATTR cardiac amyloidosis without endomyocardial biopsy, which has transformed how this once-underdiagnosed cause of HFpEF is recognised.

🚩 A positive bone scan alone does NOT diagnose ATTR. AL amyloid can occasionally take up tracer too, and AL is a haematological emergency. You MUST exclude a monoclonal protein with serum & urine immunofixation AND serum free light chains BEFORE calling it ATTR.
☢️⁹⁹ᵐTc-DPD
3,3-diphosphono-1,2-propanodicarboxylic acid — the standard bone-avid tracer in the UK & Europe for ATTR imaging.
☢️⁹⁹ᵐTc-PYP
Pyrophosphate — the equivalent bone tracer used predominantly in the United States.
☢️⁹⁹ᵐTc-HMDP
Hydroxymethylene diphosphonate — a further validated bone-avid alternative.
🫀ATTR amyloid
Wild-type (older men, HFpEF, carpal tunnel) or hereditary; the target that avidly binds tracer.
1Who to scan — the clinical trigger

Suspect cardiac amyloid and request the scan in the right patient. Localisation depends on the tracer's affinity for the calcium-rich amyloid deposits (microcalcification) within ATTR-infiltrated myocardium.

Unexplained LV wall thickening (LVH) with HFpEF, especially in a man ≥65→Think ATTR — request bone scintigraphy
LOW or normal ECG voltages DESPITE a thick-walled ventricle on echo→Voltage–mass mismatch, a classic amyloid clue
Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome (often years earlier)
Lumbar spinal stenosis, biceps tendon rupture
Aortic stenosis with disproportionate symptoms; intolerance of ACE inhibitors / beta-blockers
2How the study is performed

An IV injection of the bone-avid tracer is given, then imaging is delayed to let blood-pool activity clear and myocardial retention become apparent.

Whole-body / thoracic planar images acquired at 1 hour (some protocols 3 hours) after injection
SPECT (or SPECT/CT) of the chest is essential to confirm uptake is genuinely myocardial and not overlying rib/blood-pool activity
No thyroid blockade, fasting, or special prep is required
📷 Image placeholder — planar chest image showing diffuse myocardial tracer uptake exceeding rib/bone activity, with paired SPECT confirming a myocardial distribution.
3Reading the scan — Perugini grade & H:CL ratio

Uptake is scored visually and can be quantified against the contralateral chest.

Perugini grade 0 — no cardiac uptake, normal bone uptake (negative)
Grade 1 — cardiac uptake LESS than bone (equivocal)
Grade 2 — cardiac uptake EQUAL to bone (positive)
Grade 3 — cardiac uptake GREATER than bone, with attenuated/absent bone signal (positive)
Heart : contralateral (H:CL) ratio — a ratio ≥ 1.5 at 1 hour supports ATTR
Perugini grade 2 or 3 uptake→Positive for cardiac ATTR — PROVIDED monoclonal protein screen is negative
4The mandatory AL rule-out — non-biopsy diagnosis

The diagnostic algorithm couples the scan with plasma-cell screening. A grade 2–3 scan with a completely negative monoclonal screen has >99% specificity for ATTR and needs no biopsy.

Serum free light chains (kappa:lambda ratio) — must be normal
Serum immunofixation — no monoclonal band
Urine immunofixation — no Bence Jones protein
Positive scan BUT any abnormal light chains / paraprotein→Do NOT diagnose ATTR — refer to haematology & proceed to biopsy to exclude AL
🎓 Confirmed ATTR should still have TTR genotyping to separate hereditary (hATTR) from wild-type (wtATTR), as it guides family screening and therapy (e.g. tafamidis).
🚩 Radiation note: the effective dose is modest, roughly 3–6 mSv (comparable to a standard bone scan). As with all radionuclide studies it is relatively contraindicated in pregnancy, and breastfeeding may need brief interruption per local protocol — but ATTR is overwhelmingly a disease of older patients so this rarely arises.

Three-phase bone scintigraphy is a functional nuclear-medicine study using ⁹⁹ᵐTc-labelled diphosphonate (usually MDP, methylene diphosphonate) that acquires images at three separate time points after a single intravenous injection. It exploits the fact that osteomyelitis alters both local blood flow and osteoblastic bone turnover, whereas superficial soft-tissue infection (cellulitis) alters flow alone. Its great strength is early sensitivity — becoming positive within 24–48h of infection, well before plain-film changes appear.

☢️⁹⁹ᵐTc-MDP
Diphosphonate chemisorbed onto hydroxyapatite at sites of active osteoblastic mineralisation; γ-emitter, 140 keV, half-life ~6h.
🩸Phase 1 — Flow
Dynamic angiographic images over the first ~60s; reflects regional arterial perfusion/hyperaemia.
💧Phase 2 — Blood pool
Immediate static image at ~5 min; tracer in the extravascular soft-tissue compartment, shows hyperaemia/inflammation.
🦴Phase 3 — Delayed bone
Static images at 2–4h once soft-tissue clears; focal uptake = osteoblastic bone involvement. The discriminating phase.
1Indication

Suspected osteomyelitis, particularly in a bone with a normal or equivocal plain radiograph and no metalwork. Especially useful in the paediatric long bone, the diabetic foot, and to distinguish deep bone infection from overlying soft-tissue infection.

Acute osteomyelitis with negative/early X-ray.
Differentiating osteomyelitis from cellulitis.
Suspected multifocal or occult bony infection.
2Technique

Little patient preparation is needed. The patient is well hydrated. A bolus of ⁹ᵐTc-MDP (~500–600 MBq in an adult) is injected intravenously with the gamma camera already positioned over the region of interest so the flow phase is captured. An immediate blood-pool static is then acquired at ~5 minutes. The patient voids and returns at 2–4 hours for delayed images; SPECT or SPECT/CT can be added for anatomical localisation.

Positive in ALL 3 phases→Osteomyelitis
Phases 1 & 2 positive, delayed NOT focal→Cellulitis / soft-tissue infection
📷 Image placeholder — three-panel bone scan of a foot showing focal increased uptake on flow, blood-pool and delayed images at the same site (positive three-phase study).
3What you look for

Compare the three phases at the site of concern, always against the contralateral normal side.

Osteomyelitis: focal increased uptake persisting and often intensifying through all three phases — flow, blood pool AND delayed bone image.
Cellulitis: increased flow and blood-pool activity but only diffuse, non-focal delayed activity with no true bony uptake.
Normal: symmetric perfusion, no focal blood-pool blush, symmetric physiological skeletal uptake on delayed images.
4Pitfalls & adjuncts

Sensitivity for osteomyelitis is high, but specificity is limited wherever bone turnover is already raised — recent surgery, fracture, orthopaedic hardware, or a neuropathic (Charcot) joint in the diabetic foot — all of which can be positive on all three phases without infection.

In equivocal or post-surgical cases add a labelled white-cell scan (⁹ᵐTc-HMPAO or ¹¹¹In-oxine leucocytes) — accumulates in infection, not in bland bone remodelling.
Combine with a marrow (sulfur colloid) study to separate infection from displaced/expanded marrow (Charcot).
🚩 A positive three-phase scan is NOT specific for infection near recent fracture, surgery or metalwork — correlate clinically and escalate to labelled-WBC imaging before committing to a diagnosis of osteomyelitis.
🎓 Classic exam discriminator: osteomyelitis is hot on all three phases; cellulitis is hot on the first two but cold (no focal uptake) on the delayed bone phase. The delayed phase is what tells you the bone itself is involved.
🚩 Radiation & pregnancy: effective dose is a few mSv. Avoid in pregnancy unless benefit outweighs risk; if breastfeeding, no established interruption is generally required for MDP but local guidance and close-contact minimisation apply. Encourage hydration and frequent voiding to reduce bladder dose.
NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL__Nuclear — Rena:
The isotope renogram is a dynamic renal scintigraphy study: a gamma-camera captures a continuous sequence of images over the kidneys after IV injection of a radiotracer, generating both split (differential) renal function (the % contribution of each kidney) and a time-activity renogram curve for each kidney. It answers two clinical questions imaging alone cannot: is a dilated collecting system truly obstructed, and is hypertension driven by renal artery stenosis?

☢️⁹⁹ᵐTc-MAG3
Actively secreted by proximal tubules; high extraction, so gives superior images and remains the preferred agent, especially in poor renal function.
☢️⁹⁹ᵐTc-DTPA
Cleared by glomerular filtration; a true GFR marker but poorer image quality in impaired kidneys — the second-line dynamic tracer.
💧F+20 diuretic
IV frusemide given to challenge a dilated system — washout means no obstruction, non-washout means true obstruction.
💊Captopril
ACE inhibitor unmasks a functionally significant renal artery stenosis by removing efferent arteriolar vasoconstriction.
1Indications
Obstruction — is a hydronephrotic / dilated pelvicalyceal system (e.g. PUJ obstruction) truly obstructing outflow, or a baggy but free-draining system? Assessed with the diuretic (F+20 / frusemide) renogram.
Renovascular hypertension — suspected renal artery stenosis as a cause of secondary/resistant hypertension, assessed with captopril renography.
Split function — quantifying each kidney's relative contribution before nephrectomy, in a poorly-functioning or duplex kidney, or after transplant.
2Technique & preparation
Hydration: patient well hydrated (oral fluids ± IV) — dehydration mimics obstruction by slowing washout. Ask patient to void immediately before imaging; a full bladder can cause back-pressure and false non-washout.
Injection & acquisition: IV bolus of ⁹⁹ᵐTc-MAG3 (or DTPA) with the patient supine (or sitting) under the gamma camera positioned posteriorly. Dynamic planar images are acquired continuously for ~20–30 minutes.
Curve generation: regions of interest are drawn over each kidney to produce time-activity (renogram) curves and to compute split function from uptake in the 1–2.5 minute phase.
Dilated system, unsure if obstructed→give IV frusemide (F+20 = 20 min after tracer, or F0 / F−15 protocols) and watch for washout
Hypertension, query renovascular→captopril (or enalaprilat) renogram ± a baseline study for comparison
📷 Image placeholder — posterior dynamic renogram frames with paired kidney time-activity curves and the diuretic arrow marked on the x-axis.
3Curve interpretation
Normal: a sharp rise (uptake phase), a peak at ~3–5 min, then a steady fall (excretion phase) as tracer drains to the bladder.
Obstructed: a continuously rising curve that plateaus and does NOT fall, and crucially fails to wash out after frusemide — the hallmark of true obstruction.
Baggy / non-obstructed dilated system: curve rises and holds, but PROMPTLY washes out once frusemide is given — dilatation without obstruction.
Poor function: a flat, low-amplitude curve with reduced tracer uptake and a low split function on that side.
Renovascular (positive captopril study): ACE inhibition worsens the affected kidney's curve — delayed time-to-peak, delayed excretion and a fall in its relative uptake compared with baseline.
Rising curve, no washout after frusemide→true mechanical obstruction
4Safety, radiation & precautions
Radiation: low effective dose (roughly 0.5–1 mSv for a MAG3 study) — comparable to a few months of background radiation and less than a CT urogram.
Renal impairment: no iodinated contrast is used, so there is no contrast nephrotoxicity risk — an advantage over CT/IVU; MAG3 is preferred when function is poor.
Captopril studies: withhold ACE inhibitors/ARBs beforehand per protocol, ensure hydration, and monitor for hypotension after the captopril dose.
🚩 Pregnancy: defer if possible — exclude pregnancy before injecting a radiopharmaceutical (ideally schedule in the first 10 days of the cycle). Breastfeeding: ⁹⁹ᵐTc-MAG3 usually requires only a short interruption/expression of milk per local guidance. Avoid frusemide in significant hypovolaemia/hypotension and captopril where ACE inhibition is contraindicated.
🎓 The classic exam distinction: a dilated system that washes out after frusemide is NOT obstructed (baggy PUJ), whereas a rising curve that fails to wash out IS obstructed. MAG3 is secreted (better images), DTPA is filtered (true GFR).

The ⁹⁹ᵐTc-DMSA (dimercaptosuccinic acid) scan is a static cortical renal study and the gold-standard test for imaging functioning renal parenchyma. Roughly 40–50% of injected tracer binds to proximal tubular cells of the renal cortex and is retained, so the images map viable cortex directly — making DMSA the best test for detecting cortical scarring and for measuring split (differential) function between the two kidneys.

1Tracer & mechanism
⁹⁹ᵐTc-DMSA is injected intravenously; ~1–2 MBq/kg in children (typical adult dose ~80 MBq).
It is taken up and fixed in proximal tubular cells of the cortex, with minimal collecting-system excretion — giving clean cortical images without pelvicalyceal activity obscuring the parenchyma.
Because retention reflects functioning tubular mass, uptake is a true marker of viable cortex, unlike dynamic tracers that mainly show drainage.
Need best cortical detail & split function→DMSA (static cortical)
2Indications
☢️Cortical scarring
Detecting scars after recurrent UTIs / pyelonephritis, especially with vesicoureteric reflux (VUR).
☢️Acute pyelonephritis
Confirming acute infection as photopenic (cold) defects without volume loss.
☢️Split function
Quantifying differential function (each kidney's % contribution) before surgery.
☢️Ectopic / anomalous
Locating ectopic, duplex or horseshoe kidneys and assessing functioning moieties.
2Technique & timing
Prep: good hydration; no specific fasting or thyroid blockade required.
Timing: imaging performed ~2–4 hours after injection to allow cortical fixation and background clearance.
Acquisition: planar posterior + posterior-oblique views with a gamma camera; SPECT may improve scar detection. Split function is computed from relative counts in each kidney.
Scarring vs acute: assessment for permanent scarring is delayed several months (usually ≥ 4–6 months) after an acute infection, so acute inflammatory change is not mistaken for a fixed scar.
Recent febrile UTI, imaging now→Shows acute change — rescan months later for scar
📷 Image placeholder — posterior planar DMSA showing a wedge-shaped photopenic cortical defect at the upper pole of the left kidney with reduced split function.
4Findings & safety
Normal: smooth, homogeneous cortical uptake in both kidneys with symmetrical outlines; split function close to 50:50 (normal range ~45–55%).
Acute pyelonephritis: focal or multifocal cold (photopenic) defects with preserved renal outline / no volume loss.
Scarring: focal cortical defect with volume loss / cortical thinning and flattening of the contour — classically wedge-shaped, often at the poles.
Safety: low effective dose (~1 mSv order); a small radiation exposure justified by the diagnostic yield in recurrent infection.
🚩 Pregnancy is a relative contraindication — confirm pregnancy status in those of childbearing potential. Advise interrupting breastfeeding briefly after ⁹⁹ᵐTc administration per local protocol, and always use weight-based paediatric dosing to minimise dose.
🎓 Cold defect + preserved volume/outline = acute pyelonephritis; cold defect + volume loss/cortical thinning = established scar. Wait several months post-infection before labelling a defect a permanent scar.

Thyroid scintigraphy is functional imaging that maps how thyroid tissue handles iodine-like tracers, answering a question anatomical imaging cannot: is a gland or a nodule working? Its two headline jobs are characterising the cause of thyrotoxicosis and stratifying thyroid nodules by function, because uptake pattern points directly to the underlying pathology and to management.

1Tracer & mechanism of localisation

Two radiopharmaceuticals dominate. Both exploit the sodium-iodide symporter (NIS) on thyroid follicular cells.

☢️⁹⁹ᵐTc-pertechnetate
Trapped by NIS but NOT organified. Cheap, short half-life (6h), imaged at ~20 min. First-line for most thyrotoxicosis work-up.
☢️¹²³I (iodine-123)
Trapped AND organified — mirrors true iodine handling. Better lesion characterisation and for retrosternal/ectopic tissue; imaged at several hours.
🧭NIS uptake
Functioning tissue concentrates tracer; non-functioning tissue does not. Uptake = function, not anatomy.
🎓 Because pertechnetate is trapped but never organified, it cannot be used to detect organification defects (e.g. Pendred syndrome) — for that you need radioiodine with a perchlorate discharge test.
2Indications & patient preparation
Characterise thyrotoxicosis — distinguish Graves', toxic adenoma, toxic multinodular goitre and thyroiditis when biochemistry (suppressed TSH, raised free T4/T3) confirms the state but not the cause.
Assess a nodule by function — determine whether a palpable or scan-detected nodule is hot (autonomous) or cold (hypofunctioning).
Ectopic / retrosternal tissue — locate lingual thyroid or substernal extension.
Recent iodinated CT contrast or amiodarone→Iodine load floods NIS & blunts uptake — defer the scan (weeks for contrast, months for amiodarone)
On carbimazole / propylthiouracil or levothyroxine→Antithyroid drugs and exogenous thyroxine alter uptake — check local protocol on withholding
📷 Image placeholder — describe the planar gamma-camera acquisition of the neck with the patient supine, neck extended.
3Technique — how the study is performed
Administration — IV ⁹⁹ᵐTc-pertechnetate (or oral/IV ¹²³I).
Positioning — supine, neck extended over a pillow.
Imaging — planar images with a gamma camera (± pinhole collimator for magnified nodule views) at ~20 min for pertechnetate, later for iodine. Anterior and oblique views.
Quantification — % uptake can be calculated to grade gland activity and inform radioiodine therapy dosing.

SPECT is occasionally added for retrosternal or anatomically complex tissue, but planar imaging answers most clinical questions.

4Reading the scan — hot vs cold patterns
🔥Diffuse increased uptake
Graves' disease — homogeneously avid, enlarged gland.
🔆Single hot nodule
Toxic adenoma — one avid focus with suppressed uptake in the rest of the gland.
🗺️Patchy hot & cold areas
Toxic multinodular goitre — heterogeneous uptake across an enlarged gland.
🚫Near-absent uptake
Thyroiditis (de Quervain's, silent/post-partum), factitious thyrotoxicosis, iodine load, or recent amiodarone.
Thyrotoxic patient + globally suppressed (near-absent) uptake→Think destructive thyroiditis or exogenous thyroxine — NOT Graves'; treatment is supportive, not antithyroid drugs or radioiodine
Solitary nodule that is COLD (hypofunctioning)→Slightly higher malignancy risk — proceed to ultrasound-guided FNA
🚩 A hot nodule is almost always benign, but a cold nodule carries a modestly increased malignancy risk and warrants FNA cytology. Scintigraphy grades function — it does not exclude cancer.
5Safety & radiation
Low dose — ⁹⁹ᵐTc-pertechnetate delivers a low effective dose (~1 mSv order); ¹²³I is also low, and ¹³¹I is avoided for diagnostics because of its higher dose.
Pregnancy — a contraindication; radiopharmaceutical crosses the placenta and the fetal thyroid concentrates iodine after ~10–12 weeks. Exclude pregnancy before scanning.
Breastfeeding — interrupt/cease per local protocol (longer for radioiodine than for pertechnetate).
🚩 Recent iodinated contrast or amiodarone saturates NIS and produces a falsely low uptake — always ask about these before booking, or the scan is uninterpretable.

Radioactive iodine studies exploit the thyroid follicular cell's unique ability to trap iodide through the sodium-iodide symporter (NIS) and organify it into thyroid hormone. This makes iodine radioisotopes both a diagnostic probe of thyroid function (the radioactive iodine uptake, RAIU, scan) and a targeted therapeutic agent. ¹²³I is a pure gamma emitter ideal for imaging and uptake measurement; ¹³&sup9;I emits beta particles that deliver a lethal local radiation dose to functioning thyroid tissue, making it the workhorse for treating hyperthyroidism and ablating differentiated thyroid cancer.

☢️Iodine-123 (¹²³I)
Pure gamma emitter, ~13 h half-life. Trapped & organified; used for diagnostic uptake and thyroid/whole-body imaging with low dose.
☢️Iodine-131 (¹³&sup9;I)
Beta & gamma emitter, ~8 day half-life. Beta particles ablate tissue — therapy for Graves', toxic nodules and thyroid cancer; also whole-body scans.
🔬Technetium-99m pertechnetate
Alternative tracer: trapped by NIS but NOT organified. Cheap, quick imaging — but uptake and organification differ from true iodine.
🧪rhTSH (Thyrogen)
Recombinant TSH used to stimulate iodine uptake before cancer ablation/scanning without needing thyroid hormone withdrawal.
1Indications

Radioiodine spans diagnosis and therapy across benign and malignant thyroid disease.

RAIU / diagnostic scan: differentiate causes of thyrotoxicosis (high vs low uptake), assess a solitary nodule ('hot' vs 'cold'), and evaluate ectopic or retrosternal thyroid tissue.
¹³&sup9;I therapy for hyperthyroidism: definitive treatment of Graves' disease and toxic nodular goitre / toxic adenoma, especially after relapse or drug intolerance.
¹³&sup9;I therapy for cancer: ablation of the post-thyroidectomy remnant and treatment of iodine-avid nodal / distant metastases in differentiated (papillary/follicular) thyroid carcinoma.
Whole-body iodine scan: surveillance of treated thyroid cancer to detect residual or recurrent iodine-avid disease, interpreted alongside thyroglobulin.
Thyrotoxic patient, need to know the cause→RAIU scan — high uptake vs low uptake splits the differential
2Technique & patient preparation

A small oral tracer dose of ¹²³I (or ¹³&sup9;I) is given; a gamma probe or camera measures the counts over the neck, expressed as a percentage of the administered dose.

Timing: uptake is typically measured at an early point (4–6 h) and again at 24 h; a background reference is used to calculate the true fraction retained.
Diet & drugs: a low-iodine diet beforehand and avoidance of recent iodinated contrast, amiodarone and kelp/supplements, which flood the gland and suppress uptake. Antithyroid drugs (carbimazole/PTU) are stopped for several days as appropriate.
Imaging modes: planar gamma imaging shows the distribution; SPECT adds cross-sectional detail. For cancer follow-up, a whole-body scan is done after therapy withdrawal or rhTSH stimulation.
📷 Image placeholder — planar thyroid uptake scan comparing diffuse homogeneous Graves' uptake with a focal 'hot' toxic nodule suppressing the rest of the gland.
3Uptake interpretation

The single most useful split in a thyrotoxic patient is whether uptake is HIGH or LOW.

High, diffuse uptake across the whole gland→Graves' disease
High, focal uptake with suppressed surrounding tissue→Toxic adenoma / toxic multinodular goitre
Low / near-absent uptake in a thyrotoxic patient→Thyroiditis (subacute/de Quervain, postpartum), iodine load, or factitious thyroxine ingestion
A 'cold' nodule (reduced uptake) on a scan of a solitary nodule carries a higher risk of malignancy and warrants further assessment; a 'hot' autonomous nodule is almost always benign.
Low uptake from an iodine load (contrast, amiodarone) is a technical/physiological cause — not true gland failure — and also makes radioiodine therapy ineffective until the iodine washes out.
4Radioiodine therapy & safety

Therapeutic ¹³&sup9;I is given orally; its beta emission destroys functioning tissue over subsequent weeks, with hypothyroidism the expected long-term outcome after treating hyperthyroidism.

Radiation protection: after therapy patients follow time-limited precautions — keep distance from young children and pregnant women, minimise close prolonged contact, and follow local hygiene advice until the dose falls.
Conception: pregnancy must be avoided for around 6 months afterwards (both sexes counselled), and future fertility discussed.
Thyroid eye disease: radioiodine can precipitate or worsen Graves' orbitopathy, particularly in smokers; steroid cover may be given and it may be avoided in active moderate-to-severe eye disease.
Preparation: antithyroid drugs are stopped beforehand to allow uptake, and a low-iodine diet is used to maximise avidity for cancer ablation.
🚩 Pregnancy and breastfeeding are ABSOLUTE contraindications to radioiodine — it crosses the placenta and is concentrated in fetal thyroid and breast milk. A pregnancy test is mandatory before administration in women of childbearing age, and breastfeeding must be stopped.
🎓 Exam rule of thumb: in thyrotoxicosis, HIGH uptake = Graves' or toxic nodular disease (treatable with radioiodine), LOW uptake = thyroiditis or iodine load / factitious (radioiodine will not work). Match the uptake pattern to the mechanism before choosing therapy.

Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA) cytology is the pivotal test for characterising a thyroid nodule after clinical and sonographic assessment. It is a minimally invasive, outpatient procedure that samples cells (not tissue architecture) from a nodule to triage patients toward reassurance, repeat sampling, diagnostic surgery, or definitive cancer treatment. In the UK the cytology is reported using the Royal College of Pathologists (RCPath) "Thy" classification, layered on top of a sonographic risk score.

1Risk-stratify by ultrasound first (U/TIRADS)

Every palpable or incidental nodule is first characterised on grey-scale ultrasound before any needle is passed. The British Thyroid Association (BTA) "U" system grades nodules U1–U5, mirrored by TIRADS scoring elsewhere.

U1 — normal.
U2 — benign (cystic, spongiform, halo, peripheral eggshell calcification).
U3 — indeterminate/equivocal.
U4 — suspicious (hypoechoic, irregular margin).
U5 — malignant (microcalcification, taller-than-wide shape, infiltration, abnormal nodes).
U3–U5 nodule→proceed to US-guided FNA for cytology

Sonographic features that raise suspicion include marked hypoechogenicity, a taller-than-wide (anteroposterior > transverse) shape, irregular/lobulated margins, and punctate microcalcification.

2Perform the US-guided FNA

Real-time ultrasound guidance is standard: it directs the needle into the most suspicious part of the nodule (solid, vascular component), avoids cystic/necrotic areas that yield non-diagnostic samples, and improves adequacy over palpation-guided sampling. A fine (23–27G) needle is passed under continuous sonographic visualisation; several passes are smeared onto slides and/or rinsed into liquid-based cytology medium. No anaesthetic or minimal local anaesthetic is needed and the patient can go home immediately.

📷 Image placeholder — ultrasound screen showing a hypoechoic thyroid nodule with the bright echogenic FNA needle tip advanced into it, alongside a stained cytology slide of aspirated follicular cells.
🎓 Aspiration of frankly bloodstained fluid that recurs after drainage, or a residual solid mural nodule in a cystic lesion, warrants re-sampling of the solid component — pure cyst fluid is often acellular and non-diagnostic (Thy1c).
3Report with the RCPath "Thy" classification

The cytopathologist assigns a Thy grade reflecting the probability of malignancy. The critical conceptual point: cytology samples loose cells and cannot assess capsular or vascular invasion, so it cannot distinguish a follicular adenoma from a follicular carcinoma — that distinction requires histology of the resected nodule capsule.

🩸Thy1 / Thy1c
Non-diagnostic / inadequate (Thy1c = cystic). Insufficient follicular cells → repeat US-guided FNA.
✅Thy2 / Thy2c
Non-neoplastic / benign (Thy2c = cystic benign). Colloid nodule, thyroiditis → reassure & discharge or surveillance.
⚠️Thy3a
Atypia / possible neoplasm. Not clearly benign → repeat FNA or MDT review; some proceed to diagnostic surgery.
🔬Thy3f
Follicular neoplasm. Cannot separate adenoma from carcinoma on cytology → diagnostic hemithyroidectomy for capsule histology.
❓Thy4
Suspicious of malignancy. Features favour but are not diagnostic of cancer → surgery (hemithyroidectomy/total).
🔴Thy5
Diagnostic of malignancy (papillary, medullary, anaplastic, lymphoma, metastasis) → definitive cancer treatment.
4Map the grade to management
Thy1 / Thy1c→repeat US-guided FNA (a second non-diagnostic result prompts surgery/close follow-up)
Thy2 / Thy2c→benign — reassure, discharge or interval ultrasound
Thy3f (follicular neoplasm)→diagnostic hemithyroidectomy — capsular/vascular invasion on histology defines carcinoma
Thy4 / Thy5→surgery ± radioiodine; total thyroidectomy for confirmed/high-risk malignancy
🚩 A benign (Thy2) cytology does NOT override a suspicious ultrasound or worrying clinical picture (rapid growth, fixed mass, hoarseness, cervical lymphadenopathy). Discordant results should be taken to the thyroid MDT and the nodule re-sampled or excised — sampling error can miss a small focus of carcinoma.

Isotope (nuclear) GFR is the reference method for measured glomerular filtration rate. A tiny IV dose of a radiolabelled tracer that is freely filtered at the glomerulus — but neither secreted nor reabsorbed by the tubules — is injected, and its disappearance from the plasma is tracked with a few timed blood samples. The rate at which the plasma clears the tracer is the GFR. Because it measures real handling of a filtered marker rather than inferring it from a surrogate, it is far more accurate than creatinine-based eGFR and is used wherever a precise number genuinely changes management.

☢️⁵¹Cr-EDTA
Chromium-51 labelled EDTA. Freely filtered, not secreted or reabsorbed. Long-standing UK reference tracer; γ-emitter, half-life ~27.7 days.
☢️⁹⁹ᵐTc-DTPA
Technetium-99m DTPA. Also freely filtered; short 6 h half-life and lower dose. Small tubular/protein-binding effects make it marginally less pure than ⁵¹Cr-EDTA.
🧪Ideal marker
Inulin is the classic gold standard but needs a continuous infusion. Isotope tracers give the same physiology from a single bolus.
📐Result
Reported as GFR corrected to body surface area, in mL/min/1.73m², allowing comparison between patients of different size.
1Principle — clearance of a pure filtration marker

GFR is defined as the volume of plasma cleared of a substance per unit time. If a tracer is freely filtered and undergoes no tubular secretion or reabsorption, then the only route it leaves the blood is glomerular filtration — so its plasma clearance equals the GFR exactly.

Freely filtered: small, water-soluble, not protein-bound → crosses the glomerular filter unhindered.
Not secreted / not reabsorbed: tubules ignore it, so plasma disappearance reflects filtration alone.
Plasma (not urinary) clearance: the dose is known, so tracking the fall in plasma concentration over time gives clearance without needing a urine collection.
2Method — bolus, timed samples, slope-intercept

A single accurately-measured IV bolus of tracer is given, ideally weighed pre- and post-injection so the exact administered activity is known. Timed venous blood samples are then drawn from the opposite arm — a common UK protocol takes samples at roughly 2, 3 and 4 hours post-injection (a multi-sample or extended protocol is used if renal function is poor).

Plot log(plasma activity) vs time→terminal slope + intercept give clearance; GFR = dose / area under the curve
Plasma concentration falls exponentially; the terminal (slow) slope reflects renal clearance.
A correction factor (e.g. Brøchner-Mortensen) adjusts the single-pool estimate for the early fast distribution phase.
Result is then normalised to body surface area and reported in mL/min/1.73m².
📷 Image placeholder — semi-log plasma clearance curve: log counts on the y-axis against time, straight terminal slope fitted through the timed samples.
3Why it beats eGFR — and when that matters

Creatinine-based eGFR is an estimate that assumes an average relationship between creatinine and muscle mass. Isotope GFR measures the physiology directly, so it is the number to trust when a wrong value would harm the patient.

💊Chemo dosing
Precise GFR before nephrotoxic agents, especially carboplatin dosed by the Calvert formula (dose = AUC × (GFR + 25)).
🫘Kidney donor
Work-up of a potential living kidney donor, where true split/total function must be documented before nephrectomy.
🧒Children
Paediatric oncology and nephrology, where creatinine equations are unreliable and accuracy is critical.
💪Odd muscle mass
Extremes of muscle mass, amputees, bodybuilders, cachexia or malnutrition — anywhere creatinine misrepresents function.
4Limitations, safety & radiation

The technique is robust but depends entirely on accurate timing and volumes. Errors in the injected dose, sample times or a missed extravasated injection all corrupt the slope and the calculated GFR.

Oedema, ascites or gross extracellular fluid overload→tracer distributes into the expanded ECF → delayed equilibration and an unreliable result (extended sampling needed)
Radiation dose is very low — of the order of a fraction of a millisievert, far less than a CT — but it is still ionising radiation and must be justified.
Timing discipline: venous samples must be taken from the arm opposite the injection to avoid contamination from residual tracer.
Slow function / delayed equilibration needs a later or multi-sample protocol, otherwise clearance is underestimated.
🚩 Pregnancy is a relative contraindication — check pregnancy status and avoid unless the benefit clearly justifies fetal exposure. After ⁹⁹ᵐTc-DTPA, advise a short interruption of breastfeeding per local protocol. A contaminated or extravasated (tissued) injection invalidates the study and it should be rebooked.
🎓 Exam favourite: carboplatin dosing uses the Calvert formula, which needs an accurate GFR — the classic reason to request an isotope (⁵¹Cr-EDTA) GFR rather than trusting eGFR. Remember the ideal tracer is freely filtered, not secreted, not reabsorbed.
NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL__Nuclear — Card:
A ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) scan is a nuclear-medicine study that images two independent processes in the lung — where inhaled gas reaches (ventilation) and where pulmonary arterial blood flows (perfusion) — then compares the two maps. The whole diagnostic value rests on a single idea: in pulmonary embolism (PE) a clot blocks a segmental artery, so a region loses perfusion while its ventilation stays intact. That perfusion–ventilation MISMATCH is the hallmark of PE.

1The two radiopharmaceuticals & how they localise
Perfusion (Q): IV ⁹⁹ᵐTc-MAA (macroaggregated albumin) — particles ~10–90 µm are carried to the lungs and lodge (microembolise) in pulmonary capillaries & arterioles, mapping regional blood flow. Only a tiny fraction of capillaries is occluded, so it is safe.
Ventilation (V): inhaled ⁹⁹ᵐTc-Technegas (ultrafine carbon-encapsulated technetium) or the gas ⁸¹ᵐKr — distributes to alveoli, mapping where air reaches.
Perfusion defect + normal ventilation in same zone→MISMATCH = PE
Perfusion defect + matching ventilation defect→MATCHED = airway/parenchymal disease, not PE
☢️⁹⁹ᵐTc-MAA (perfusion)
IV albumin aggregates lodge in pulmonary capillaries — maps arterial blood flow.
💨⁹⁹ᵐTc-Technegas / ⁸¹ᵐKr (ventilation)
Inhaled agent reaching alveoli — maps regional airflow.
🫁MISMATCH
Q defect with preserved V — the diagnostic signature of PE.
🧩MATCHED defect
V and Q both reduced — suggests COPD, consolidation, effusion, not PE.
2Indications & when to choose it over CTPA
Main indication: suspected acute PE, especially when CTPA is contraindicated or best avoided — iodinated contrast allergy, renal impairment, or to spare radiation to breast tissue in younger women and pregnancy.
Best in patients with a NORMAL chest X-ray: a clear CXR maximises specificity. An abnormal CXR (consolidation, effusion, oedema) creates matched defects and makes the scan hard to interpret — CTPA is then preferred.
Also used for pre-operative lung-function mapping and chronic thromboembolic (CTEPH) assessment. Modern practice often uses perfusion-only imaging or SPECT V/Q for higher accuracy.
🎓 Rule of thumb: young woman, pregnant or contrast issue, plus a normal CXR → V/Q (or Q-only) is the study of choice; abnormal CXR → CTPA.
📷 Image placeholder — paired planar V and Q images showing a wedge-shaped segmental perfusion defect with preserved ventilation (mismatch) in suspected PE.
3How it is performed
Recent CXR first — needed for interpretation and patient selection.
Ventilation phase: patient inhales Technegas/⁸¹ᵐKr through a mouthpiece; images acquired in multiple projections.
Perfusion phase: ⁹⁹ᵐTc-MAA injected IV with the patient supine (to distribute particles evenly); imaging immediately after.
Planar (multiple views) vs SPECT: SPECT V/Q gives 3-D data, better sensitivity/specificity and fewer indeterminate results; increasingly standard.
4Reading the scan: probability & safety
Reported by probability (PIOPED-style): normal / low / intermediate (indeterminate) / high probability. High probability = ≥2 large segmental mismatched defects.
A NORMAL perfusion scan effectively excludes PE — a key, reassuring result.
Radiation/pregnancy: delivers a lower dose to breast tissue than CTPA, so it is often preferred in pregnancy when the CXR is normal; a reduced-dose or perfusion-only protocol further limits exposure. CTPA gives a higher fetal dose late in pregnancy but much higher maternal breast dose.
🚩 Right-to-left cardiac shunt or severe pulmonary hypertension is a caution for MAA (particles can reach the systemic/cerebral circulation) — use a reduced particle number. Known MAA/albumin hypersensitivity is a contraindication.
🎓 Intermediate/indeterminate scans are the weakness of the test — they need further imaging (CTPA) or correlation with clinical probability and D-dimer.

Myocardial perfusion imaging (MPI) with single-photon emission CT (SPECT) is a functional nuclear-medicine test of coronary blood flow. A radiotracer taken up by viable myocytes in proportion to regional perfusion is imaged after stress and again at rest; comparing the two sets distinguishes inducible ischaemia (a reversible defect) from established infarct or scar (a fixed defect), and quantifies the amount of myocardium at risk.

1The radiotracer & how it localises

Modern MPI uses a ₃₃ᵐTc-labelled agent (sestamibi or tetrofosmin), a lipophilic cation that crosses the myocyte membrane and is trapped in mitochondria in proportion to regional coronary blood flow and cell viability. Uptake therefore marks myocardium that is both perfused and alive. The older agent ²⁰¹Tl-thallium, a potassium analogue handled by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, is still used where redistribution (viability) imaging is wanted.

☢₃₃ᵐTc-sestamibi
Lipophilic cation, mitochondrial trapping; minimal redistribution so stress & rest need separate injections.
☢₃₃ᵐTc-tetrofosmin
Similar kinetics to sestamibi; fast liver clearance, good image quality, most common UK agent.
☢²⁰¹Tl-thallium
K⁺ analogue; redistributes over hours, allowing viability assessment; higher radiation dose.
2Indications
Assessment of stable chest pain / known or suspected coronary artery disease.
Determining the functional (haemodynamic) significance of a known stenosis, e.g. before revascularisation.
Myocardial viability — is dysfunctional myocardium hibernating (viable) or scarred?
Risk stratification, e.g. before major non-cardiac surgery or after MI, and follow-up of revascularised patients.
3How the study is performed — stress & rest

Two image sets are acquired — one at stress and one at rest — each after a separate tracer injection, and compared. Stress is achieved by exercise (treadmill/bicycle) or, if the patient cannot exercise adequately, pharmacologically:

💉Vasodilators
Adenosine, dipyridamole or regadenoson — dilate normal coronaries, creating flow heterogeneity (“coronary steal”) that unmasks stenosed territories.
💓Dobutamine
Inotrope/chronotrope raising myocardial oxygen demand; used when vasodilators are contraindicated (e.g. asthma).

The tracer is injected at peak stress, images acquired, then a resting injection and second acquisition are performed. Imaging is by SPECT (a gamma camera rotating around the chest to build tomographic short-axis, vertical and horizontal long-axis slices); ECG-gating additionally yields wall motion and ejection fraction. Modern protocols increasingly use PET tracers for higher resolution and quantitative flow.

📷 Image placeholder — paired stress and rest SPECT short-axis slices showing an inferolateral perfusion defect.
4Interpretation — reversible vs fixed defects

A region with reduced tracer uptake is a defect. Its behaviour between stress and rest is the key:

Abnormal on STRESS, normal at REST→REVERSIBLE defect = inducible ischaemia (flow-limiting stenosis, viable myocardium)
Abnormal on BOTH stress and rest→FIXED defect = infarct / scar (non-viable), though hibernating myocardium can mimic this
Normal uptake on stress AND rest→No significant inducible ischaemia — excellent prognosis
🎓 The territory of the defect maps to the culprit vessel: anterior/septal = LAD, inferior = RCA, lateral = circumflex. A large reversible defect or transient ischaemic dilatation of the LV cavity flags high-risk, potentially left-main or multivessel disease.
🚩 Pharmacological stress is not without hazard. Adenosine and dipyridamole are contraindicated in asthma/significant bronchospasm and in high-grade (2nd/3rd degree) AV block without a pacemaker. Patients must withhold caffeine and theophylline for ≥12–24 h beforehand (they block adenosine receptors and cause false-negative studies). Full resuscitation facilities, and aminophylline (adenosine/dipyridamole reversal), must be immediately available.
🚩 Radiation: a ₃₃ᵐTc MPI delivers roughly 6–10 mSv effective dose (thallium higher). It is justified against clinical benefit; MPI is avoided in pregnancy, and breastfeeding is briefly interrupted after ₃₃ᵐTc injection per local protocol.

MIBG (metaiodobenzylguanidine) is a structural analogue of noradrenaline (norepinephrine). Labelled with radioiodine (¹²³I for diagnostic imaging, ¹³¹I for imaging or therapy), it is taken up into adrenergic and sympathomedullary tissue via the noradrenaline transporter (NAT) and stored in neurosecretory granules. This makes it a functional tracer for catecholamine-secreting and neural-crest tumours, and the same molecule labelled with ¹³¹I can be used to deliver targeted radiotherapy — a classic theranostic pairing.

1Mechanism & indications

MIBG enters cells through the noradrenaline transporter and concentrates in tissue rich in sympathetic innervation or of neural-crest origin. Localisation is therefore functional, not purely anatomical.

Localising & staging phaeochromocytoma (adrenal medulla) and paraganglioma (extra-adrenal), especially when biochemically proven but not localised on CT/MRI, or to detect multifocal/metastatic disease.
Neuroblastoma in children — diagnosis, staging, response assessment and surveillance; the great majority of neuroblastomas are MIBG-avid.
Assessing suitability for ¹³¹I-MIBG therapy: an avid diagnostic scan predicts uptake of the therapeutic dose.
Raised metanephrines but CT/MRI shows no clear source→MIBG scan to localise the catecholamine-secreting tumour
2Patient preparation
🚩 Thyroid blockade is essential. Give potassium iodide or Lugol's iodine starting the day before injection and continuing for several days after, to saturate the thyroid and block uptake of free radioiodine, protecting it from radiation. Blockade is more prolonged when ¹³¹I is used.
Withhold interfering drugs that block or displace MIBG at the noradrenaline transporter or depleting granules: labetalol and other combined alpha/beta blockers, tricyclic antidepressants, sympathomimetics (including decongestants), and some calcium-channel blockers. These are stopped for an appropriate washout period after checking it is safe to do so.
Ensure adequate hydration and encourage voiding to reduce bladder radiation dose.
Patient on labetalol or a tricyclic antidepressant→False-negative scan — withhold before imaging
3Performing the study

MIBG is given as a slow intravenous injection (rapid injection can provoke a hypertensive/catecholamine surge). Whole-body planar images are acquired at 24 hours, with delayed images at 48 hours if needed to clarify equivocal uptake or bowel activity. SPECT/CT is frequently added to give anatomical correlation and improve lesion localisation.

📷 Image placeholder — 24-hour whole-body MIBG planar scan showing a focus of abnormal uptake at a right adrenal phaeochromocytoma, with SPECT/CT fusion inset.
4Interpreting the scan

Normal (physiological) uptake is seen in the salivary glands, myocardium, liver, spleen, bowel, and the urinary tract/bladder (excreted); mild adrenal uptake can be normal. An abnormal scan shows focal uptake outside these expected sites — a primary tumour and/or metastatic deposits in bone, nodes, liver or soft tissue.

☢️¹²³I-MIBG
Diagnostic gamma tracer; better images and lower dose than ¹³¹I-MIBG.
☢️¹³¹I-MIBG
Therapeutic beta-emitter for MIBG-avid phaeo/paraganglioma and neuroblastoma.
🧠Physiological sites
Salivary glands, myocardium, liver, spleen, bowel, bladder.
🔬&sup6;&sup8;Ga-DOTATATE
Somatostatin-receptor PET; higher sensitivity for paraganglioma & SDHB disease.

For paraganglioma (especially SDHB-related and head-and-neck disease) and for detecting small metastases, &sup6;&sup8;Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT is generally more sensitive and is increasingly first-line; MIBG remains important where ¹³¹I-MIBG therapy is being considered because it confirms avidity.

🎓 A negative MIBG scan does not exclude a phaeochromocytoma — correlate with biochemistry and cross-sectional imaging, and consider DOTATATE PET. Confirmed MIBG avidity is the gateway to ¹³¹I-MIBG radionuclide therapy.
5Radiation & pregnancy
🚩 Involves ionising radiation. Pregnancy is a contraindication (avoid unless the benefit is compelling); exclude pregnancy before injection. Breastfeeding must be interrupted — stopped for a period with ¹²³I and discontinued with ¹³¹I. Patients receiving ¹³¹I-MIBG therapy require radiation-protection isolation and contact restrictions until activity falls to safe levels.

A DaTscan is a nuclear-medicine SPECT study using the radiotracer ¹²³I-ioflupane (FP-CIT) to image the integrity of the presynaptic dopamine transporter (DAT) on nigrostriatal dopaminergic nerve terminals in the striatum. It answers one focused clinical question: is there a genuine presynaptic dopaminergic deficit? It cannot tell you which neurodegenerative parkinsonian syndrome a patient has.

1Tracer & mechanism of localisation

Ioflupane is a cocaine analogue labelled with ¹²³I (a gamma-emitter, physical half-life ≈13 h). Injected intravenously, it crosses the blood–brain barrier and binds the presynaptic DAT on the terminals of dopaminergic neurons projecting from the substantia nigra to the striatum. Tracer bound in the caudate nucleus and putamen is therefore a marker of surviving presynaptic dopaminergic terminals.

Target: presynaptic dopamine transporter (DAT), not the postsynaptic receptor.
Region of interest: striatum = caudate head + putamen.
Loss of signal = loss of terminals, i.e. a true nigrostriatal degeneration.
2Indications

The scan separates conditions with a presynaptic dopaminergic deficit from those with intact terminals.

Clinically uncertain tremor — is it PD or essential tremor?→Abnormal = degenerative parkinsonism; normal = essential tremor
Query dementia with Lewy bodies vs Alzheimer's→Reduced striatal uptake supports DLB; normal favours AD
☢️Reduced uptake
Parkinson's disease, MSA, PSP, DLB — all degenerative, all abnormal
✅Normal uptake
Essential tremor, drug-induced, vascular & psychogenic parkinsonism
🧠Dementia
Supports DLB over Alzheimer's disease
🚩 A DaTscan cannot distinguish PD from MSA or PSP — all degenerative parkinsonian syndromes reduce striatal uptake. It confirms a presynaptic deficit, not the specific disease.
3Patient prep & how the study is performed
Thyroid blockade: give potassium iodide (or perchlorate) before injection to saturate the thyroid and block uptake of any free ¹²³I⁻, protecting the gland from radiation.
Withhold interfering drugs: agents that bind or alter DAT — cocaine, some CNS stimulants (e.g. amfetamine, methylphenidate, modafinil) and certain antidepressants (bupropion) — are stopped for an appropriate washout period to avoid false results.
Injection & timing: IV ioflupane, then SPECT imaging at ~3–6 hours to allow specific striatal binding with background clearance.
Technique: tomographic SPECT of the brain (not simple planar) for the striatal detail required.
📷 Image placeholder — axial DaTscan SPECT contrasting symmetric bilateral comma-shaped striatal uptake (normal) with an asymmetric shrunken full-stop appearance (abnormal).
4Normal vs abnormal — the shapes
Symmetric crescent / "comma" in both striata→Normal — intact presynaptic terminals
Reduced, asymmetric uptake losing the putaminal tail→Abnormal — presynaptic dopaminergic deficit ("full stop"/period)
The putamen is affected earliest; the caudate is relatively spared early, so uptake shrinks from a comma to a dot/period.
Deficit is often asymmetric, worse contralateral to the more symptomatic side.
🎓 Learn the mnemonic: comma = normal, full stop = abnormal. The tracer is a cocaine analogue binding DAT, so any recent cocaine use invalidates the scan.
🚩 Radiation & pregnancy: DaTscan delivers an effective dose of roughly 4–5 mSv. It is avoided in pregnancy, and breastfeeding should be interrupted (~3–4 days) after the ¹²³I-ioflupane injection. Always ensure thyroid blockade is given.

Labelled red-blood-cell (RBC) scintigraphy is a nuclear-medicine test for obscure or occult lower gastrointestinal bleeding. The patient's own red cells are tagged with technetium-99m and re-injected; dynamic gamma-camera imaging then hunts for the moment radiolabelled blood leaks into the bowel lumen. Its great strength is sensitivity to slow, intermittent bleeds that other modalities miss.

☢️⁹⁹ᵐTc-labelled RBCs
Autologous red cells tagged with ⁹⁹ᵐTc; stay in the vascular pool so any leak into bowel shows as an off-vessel focus.
🩸GI bleed localisation
Detects rates as low as ~0.1–0.4 mL/min — more sensitive than CT angiography or catheter angiography.
⏱️Prolonged window
Imaging over hours (with delayed re-imaging) catches intermittent bleeds that are quiescent at any single snapshot.
👶⁹⁹ᵐTc-pertechnetate (Meckel's)
Different tracer, different target: taken up by ectopic gastric mucosa in a Meckel's diverticulum — classic painless PR bleed in a child.
1Indication & principle

Used to localise obscure/occult lower GI bleeding when the source is unclear, typically to guide subsequent catheter angiography or surgery. Red cells labelled with ⁹⁹ᵐTc remain within the intravascular compartment, so if blood extravasates into the gut it produces a focus of tracer that would not normally be there.

Recurrent obscure PR bleeding, OGD & colonoscopy negative→Labelled RBC scan to localise before angiography/surgery
2Labelling & technique
A blood sample is drawn and red cells are labelled with ⁹⁹ᵐTc (commonly in-vitro/modified in-vivo methods using stannous pyrophosphate), then re-injected.
Dynamic planar imaging of the abdomen begins immediately and continues over the first ~60–90 minutes.
Delayed re-imaging (up to several hours) is used if the initial study is negative, exploiting the long tracer half-life to catch an intermittent bleed.
SPECT/CT may be added to improve anatomical localisation of a focus.
📷 Image placeholder — dynamic planar sequence showing a new focus of activity appearing in the mid-abdomen and migrating along the bowel with peristalsis.
3Normal vs abnormal — the key sign

A normal study shows tracer confined to the blood pool (heart, great vessels, liver, spleen, kidneys, bladder) with no abnormal bowel activity.

A positive study shows a focus of extravasated activity that appears, increases in intensity, and moves along the bowel with peristalsis (antegrade or retrograde). This dynamic, migrating focus is the diagnostic hallmark and distinguishes true luminal blood from fixed vascular structures.

Focus that brightens and shifts along bowel over sequential frames→Active luminal GI haemorrhage — flag the region
4Strengths, limits & the Meckel's contrast

Advantage: very sensitive to slow/intermittent bleeding (down to ~0.1–0.4 mL/min) and the prolonged, repeatable imaging window catches bleeds that are quiescent during a one-off CT or catheter angiogram.

Limitation: it localises the region but not the exact cause, and rapid peristalsis can carry luminal blood away from its origin, causing mislocalisation of the bleeding site.

Meckel's scan variant: uses ⁹⁹ᵐTc-pertechnetate (free, not RBC-bound), which is taken up by ectopic gastric mucosa. It targets a Meckel's diverticulum — a classic cause of painless PR bleeding in children — appearing as a focus of activity in the right lower quadrant that arises at the same time as gastric activity. Pretreatment (e.g. an H₂ blocker) can enhance mucosal retention of the tracer.

🚩 A migrating luminal focus localises the bleed to a bowel region only — it does not identify the underlying lesion, and brisk peristalsis can transport blood away from its true source, so correlate carefully before directing surgery or angiography.
🎓 Same isotope, different agent: labelled RBCs = brisk/obscure lower GI bleed localisation in adults; free pertechnetate = Meckel's diverticulum (ectopic gastric mucosa) in a child with painless PR bleeding. Radiation dose is modest — of the order of a few mSv (comparable to routine ⁹⁹ᵐTc studies) — but pregnancy and breastfeeding still warrant justification and precautions.

The labelled white cell scan (radiolabelled leucocyte scintigraphy) is a functional nuclear-medicine study that exploits the innate homing of neutrophils to sites of active infection. The patient's own white cells are harvested, tagged with a gamma-emitting radiotracer, reinjected, and then tracked as they migrate to and accumulate wherever neutrophils are being recruited. It is the imaging test of choice for localising occult infection when structural imaging is equivocal.

☢️⁹⁹ᵐTc-HMPAO
Lipophilic chelate crosses the leucocyte membrane and is trapped intracellularly; lower radiation dose, sharper images, but shows physiological bowel/urinary/gallbladder clearance on delayed views.
☢️¹¹¹In-oxine
Oxine carries indium into the cell where it binds cytoplasmic components; very stable label with no bowel excretion, ideal for abdominal sepsis, but higher dose and poorer resolution.
🦴Marrow scan adjunct
⁹⁹ᵐTc-sulphur/nanocolloid marrow map is co-registered for suspected prosthetic joint or diabetic-foot osteomyelitis to distinguish infection from displaced marrow.
🎯Neutrophil homing
Labelled granulocytes marginate and extravasate at sites of chemotactic signalling, so uptake reflects active neutrophilic inflammation rather than mere anatomical abnormality.
1Indications & when to request
Suspected osteomyelitis, especially prosthetic joint infection and the diabetic foot, where plain films and MRI are confounded by metalwork or neuropathic change.
Suspected infected vascular graft.
Occult intra-abdominal or pelvic collection / abscess.
Assessing inflammatory bowel disease activity and extent (particularly in patients unable to tolerate endoscopy).
Pyrexia or inflammation of unknown origin when a focus cannot be localised clinically.
Painful prosthetic hip/knee, raised CRP, MRI degraded by metal artefact→Labelled WCC scan + marrow scan to confirm or exclude prosthetic joint infection
2How the study is performed
Around 40–50 mL of the patient's blood is drawn under strict aseptic, single-patient technique.
Leucocytes are separated from red cells and plasma, then labelled ex vivo with ⁹⁹ᵐTc-HMPAO or ¹¹¹In-oxine and reinjected intravenously.
Gamma-camera imaging is acquired at an early time point (e.g. ~30 min–1 h) and at delayed points (3–4 h and, with indium, up to 24 h); SPECT or SPECT/CT is added to localise uptake anatomically.
Focal uptake that increases in intensity between early and delayed images→Active infection (fresh neutrophil recruitment over time)
📷 Image placeholder — early and delayed anterior planar leucocyte images of the pelvis/foot showing a focus of increasing uptake, with the co-registered SPECT/CT slice.
3Normal vs abnormal & the key patterns
Normal distribution: physiological uptake in liver, spleen (most intense) and bone marrow; with HMPAO there is additional renal, urinary, bowel and gallbladder activity on delayed views.
Infection: focal uptake outside the normal distribution that is stable or increases in intensity and extent over time.
Prosthetic joint / osteomyelitis: leucocyte uptake that is spatially incongruent with the marrow scan (present on WCC but absent on marrow map) indicates infection rather than displaced/expanded marrow.
IBD: increasing bowel uptake maps the site and length of active disease.
4Limitations, safety & blood-handling
Labour-intensive and time-consuming: cell separation and labelling take hours and require a specialised radiopharmacy.
Less sensitive for chronic or low-grade infection, where neutrophil recruitment is limited; marrow and physiological bowel uptake can mask or mimic disease.
Radiation: an ionising study with an effective dose broadly comparable to other nuclear-medicine scans (of the order of a few mSv); ¹¹¹In-oxine delivers a higher dose than ⁹⁹ᵐTc-HMPAO.
Pregnancy is a relative contraindication (justify carefully); breastfeeding may need interruption per local radiation-protection advice.
🚩 Blood-handling hazard: re-injecting mislabelled cells into the wrong patient is potentially fatal. Rigorous single-patient identity checks, aseptic technique and universal precautions against blood-borne viruses are mandatory throughout separation, labelling and reinjection.
🎓 For suspected prosthetic joint infection or diabetic-foot osteomyelitis, always pair the labelled leucocyte scan with a ⁹⁹ᵐTc marrow scan: infection is uptake on the white-cell study that is NOT matched on the marrow map, which markedly improves specificity.

Lymphoscintigraphy maps the drainage of a tumour to its sentinel lymph node — the first node (or nodes) into which a tumour drains and therefore the first likely site of nodal metastasis. A ⁹⁹ᵐTc-labelled colloid is injected around the tumour or biopsy cavity, tracks through the lymphatics, and is trapped in the sentinel node, which is then localised by gamma imaging and, at surgery, by a hand-held gamma probe (usually combined with blue dye). It underpins sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) in breast cancer and melanoma, letting a node-negative patient avoid the morbidity of full nodal clearance.

☢️⁹⁹ᵐTc-nanocolloid
Small colloid particles enter lymphatics & are phagocytosed/trapped in the first draining node.
🔵Patent blue dye
Intra-operative visual co-localiser; stains the sentinel node & afferent lymphatic blue.
📡Gamma probe
Hand-held detector guides the surgeon to the “hot” node through a small incision.
🎯Sentinel node
First node draining the tumour — its status predicts the whole regional basin.
1Indications & rationale
Breast cancer — early invasive breast cancer with a clinically & radiologically node-negative axilla, to stage the axilla accurately.
Cutaneous melanoma — to stage the regional nodal basin (typically ≥ pT1b / thickness ≥ 0.8 mm with adverse features), guiding prognosis and adjuvant therapy.
The aim is to avoid unnecessary full nodal clearance (axillary dissection / block dissection) and its morbidity — chiefly lymphoedema, nerve injury and shoulder stiffness.
Sentinel node negative→no completion nodal dissection needed — basin spared
Sentinel node positive→guides further management (further nodal treatment, radiotherapy or surveillance)
2Technique & timing
Injection: ⁹⁹ᵐTc-nanocolloid injected around the tumour or the biopsy/tumour site (peritumoural, subdermal or periareolar for breast; intradermal around the melanoma/scar).
Dual localisation: radiotracer plus intra-operative blue dye — using both raises the sentinel-node identification rate above either alone.
Timing: imaging from minutes up to a few hours after injection; protocols use same-day (short) or day-before injection, so surgery is timed to residual node activity.
Imaging: dynamic & static planar gamma-camera images, with SPECT/CT added to give anatomical localisation of nodes.
📷 Image placeholder — planar lymphoscintigram showing an injection-site “star” artefact and a focal hot sentinel node in the axilla.
3What the scan shows
Drainage pattern: a lymphatic channel leading from the injection site to one or more focal “hot spots” — the sentinel node(s).
Number & site: confirms how many sentinel nodes there are and in which basin (e.g. axillary vs internal mammary in breast; unpredictable basins in truncal melanoma).
Aberrant / unexpected nodes: in-transit, interval or contralateral nodes, or drainage to an unanticipated basin — these would be missed without mapping.
SPECT/CT pinpoints the node relative to anatomy, aiding a targeted surgical approach and reducing operative time.
Non-visualisation of any node→re-inject / delayed imaging; rely more on blue dye & probe at surgery
4Safety, radiation & precautions
Radiation: the effective dose is low — the small administered activity of ⁹⁹ᵐTc gives a minor exposure to patient and theatre staff, well within occupational limits.
Blue dye: transient blue skin/urine staining and, importantly, a small risk of anaphylaxis to patent blue dye — the team must be prepared to treat it.
Pregnancy/breastfeeding: pregnancy is a relative contraindication; breastfeeding may need temporary interruption per local protocol.
🚩 Patent blue dye can cause anaphylaxis — pre-warn the anaesthetist, watch for hypotension & the transient artefactual drop in pulse-oximetry (SpO₂) the dye causes.
🎓 A negative sentinel node lets a patient avoid axillary/regional clearance and its lymphoedema — that morbidity-sparing is the whole point of SLNB, so quote it in exams.
